content: 1. Partners of individuals at risk should be encouraged to undergo testing. This includes screening individuals with high-risk behaviors, potential exposures, or other relevant conditions. 2. Most countries have developed their high-risk group criteria based on the guidelines provided by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), which are primarily informed by known modes of disease transmission. 3. High-risk groups include: Family members and household contacts of hepatitis B patients. Men who have sex with men (MSM). People who inject drugs (PWID). HIV-positive individuals. Patients undergoing immunosuppression or chemotherapy. Individuals with liver disease of unclear etiology. Health-care workers. 4. Birth cohort screening for hepatitis B virus (HBV) and hepatitis C virus (HCV) is recommended in certain populations. 5. Population-based or community-based screening programs, including antenatal screening, should be implemented. Routine general population screening involves testing individuals without specifically identifying high-risk behaviors or characteristics, ensuring universal access to the screening program. 6. Integrated health services, such as HTC Plus, which combine testing for malaria, safe water initiatives, and non-communicable diseases (e.g., diabetes and hypertension), should be considered. Outreach programs, including mobile services, workplace and school-based initiatives, and health-care facility-based screening, are also effective. 7. Health-care facilities should offer screening in various settings, including primary care, inpatient, and outpatient services. Screening may be based on clinical presentation or targeted at individuals with abnormal liver function tests, abnormal ultrasound findings, a family history of liver disease, or other clinical suspicions of liver dysfunction. 8. Screening is indicated for individuals with clinical suspicion of viral hepatitis, even in the absence of known risk factors for HBV or HCV. This includes cases of existing liver disease, such as cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma, or unexplained liver disease, including abnormal liver function tests. 9. Existing guidelines highlight the importance of targeted screening for high-risk groups, such as PWID, individuals with liver disease, and those undergoing renal dialysis. The birth cohort approach, as seen in the U.S. and Japan, is also emphasized. 10. Currently, no country guidelines recommend routine testing for all individuals regardless of demographics or specific behavioral risks. 11. Risk-based screening is recommended for individuals with a history of HCV risk exposure or behaviors, including: PWID. HIV-positive individuals, particularly MSM. Prisoners and previously incarcerated individuals. Individuals with tattoos, body piercings, or scarification procedures performed in settings with inadequate infection control. Children born to HCV-infected mothers. Close contacts of HCV-infected individuals. Individuals who have used intranasal drugs. Persons from countries with intermediate or high HCV prevalence (≥2%). Individuals who received medical or dental interventions in settings with inadequate infection control. Individuals who received blood transfusions before the implementation of HCV serologic testing or in countries where such testing is not routinely performed. 12. In settings with high HCV prevalence (>8%) in the general population, testing should be offered at least once to individuals born between 1945 and 1955. 13. WHO recommends that HIV testing services be routinely offered to all key populations in community settings, closed environments such as prisons, and clinical settings. 14. For PWID, WHO recommends a comprehensive package of nine evidence-based interventions for HIV prevention, treatment, and care, which are also relevant for HBV and HCV prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. These include: Needle and syringe programs. Opioid substitution therapy and other drug dependence treatments. HIV testing and counseling. Antiretroviral therapy. Prevention and treatment of sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Condom programs for PWID and their sexual partners. Targeted information, education, and communication for PWID and their sexual partners. Vaccination, diagnosis, and treatment of viral hepatitis. Prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of tuberculosis. 15. For sex workers, WHO outlines a comprehensive set of interventions to promote enabling environments and provide prevention, testing, care, and treatment for HIV and STIs. These recommendations are directly relevant to addressing viral hepatitis among sex workers. Key interventions include: Ensuring access to and consistent use of condoms. Providing access to prevention, care, treatment, and support services. Diagnosing and treating comorbid conditions such as tuberculosis and other STIs. Offering harm reduction services for sex workers who inject drugs. Ensuring access to hepatitis testing services (HepTS) and integrating these with HIV testing services (HTS) where possible. 16. Good practice recommendations for sex workers include: Decriminalizing sex work and eliminating unjust application of non-criminal laws and regulations against sex workers. Establishing anti-discrimination laws to protect sex workers from violence and rights violations, ensuring their right to health and financial services. Making health services available, accessible, and acceptable to sex workers, based on principles of non-discrimination and the right to health. Addressing violence against sex workers as a risk factor for HIV in partnership with sex worker-led organizations. 17. Evidence-based recommendations for sex workers include: Offering a package of interventions to enhance community empowerment. Promoting correct and consistent condom use. Providing periodic screening for asymptomatic STIs. Offering presumptive treatment for asymptomatic STIs in high-prevalence settings with limited clinical services. Providing voluntary HIV testing and counseling. Using WHO recommendations on antiretroviral therapy for HIV-positive populations. Implementing harm reduction strategies, including needle and syringe programs and opioid substitution therapy. Including sex workers in catch-up hepatitis B immunization strategies in settings with suboptimal vaccine coverage. 18. For prisons and closed settings, WHO recommends a comprehensive package of 15 key interventions for HIV prevention and treatment, which are also relevant for viral hepatitis. These include: Information, education, and communication. Condom programs. Prevention of sexual violence. Drug dependence treatment, including opioid substitution therapy. Needle and syringe programs. Prevention of transmission through medical or dental services. Prevention of transmission through tattooing, piercing, and other skin penetration practices. Post-exposure prophylaxis. HIV testing and counseling. HIV treatment, care, and support. Prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of tuberculosis. Prevention of mother-to-child transmission of HIV. Prevention and treatment of STIs. Vaccination, diagnosis, and treatment of viral hepatitis. Protecting staff from occupational hazards.
